observation: Adamczyk & Bailey (2004) and Iqbal & Bailey (2007/2008), with a 2024/2025 replication (Powers & Scerbo), found interruptions at coarse task boundaries (between subtask chunks) cost close to zero resumption penalty, while interruptions at fine boundaries (mid-subtask) significantly increase resumption time and workload; the 2024/2025 study found the effect depends on the task's own internal chunking, not just objective task boundaries.
claim: Riemann should use the abstraction tree's own structure (crossing an L2 section boundary, reaching L1, a settled dial) as the breakpoint model for any interruption, since it already encodes the coarse/fine distinction this literature depends on.
mechanism: Resumption cost is driven by where in the task's internal chunk structure an interruption lands, not by interruption presence alone.
context: lab tasks, decades of replication plus a 2024/2025 replication

implications.text: Use the abstraction tree's own boundaries (L2 section crossed, dial settled at a stable level) as the coarse-breakpoint signal gating any real-time interruption.

observation: Mark, Gudith & Klocke (2008, CHI) found interrupted knowledge workers completed tasks about as fast or slightly faster than uninterrupted ones (they compensate by working faster), but at measurably higher stress, frustration, and effort — a cost invisible to a naive 'did it take longer' metric.
claim: Riemann should not measure interruption cost only by elapsed time; a silent-log item that costs no measured delay can still be experienced as costly if it steals attention at the wrong moment.
mechanism: People compensate for interruption by working faster, which hides the true cost in subjective stress/effort rather than in task completion time.
context: real workplace field study, 2008, pre-smartphone-notification era

implications.text: Track/ask about stress or frustration alongside timing when evaluating interruption tiers, not elapsed time alone.

observation: Fitz, Kushlev et al. (2019, N=237, 3-week randomized field experiment) found batching phone notifications ~3x/day reduced stress and raised wellbeing versus as-they-arrive delivery; hourly batching showed little benefit over the status quo; disabling notifications entirely increased anxiety and FOMO.
claim: A scheduled, predictable check-in batch — not zero interruption and not always-on — is the sweet spot; the 'mention at next check-in' tier should be a predictable cadence, not merely 'whenever the app is reopened.'
mechanism: Predictability of the batch, not just infrequency, drove the wellbeing gain; complete removal of interruption removed a wanted external cue and increased anxiety.

implications.text: Make the 'mention at next check-in' tier a scheduled, predictable cadence the user sets, not purely triggered by reopening the app.

observation: Altmann & Trafton's memory-for-goals model and related studies found a suspended task's goal activation decays over time, and cues encoded at the moment of suspension (not generic markers) speed re-retrieval; a 'last action taken' cue and a 'next action to do' cue were found roughly equally effective, both beating no cue.
claim: Resume-cards should be captured at the moment of pause/interruption (snapshotting the centered passage, zoom level, and a one-line recap), not reconstructed later from logs, since suspension-time context is what primes fastest recall.
mechanism: Cues present at encoding time (when the goal was suspended) are what speed later re-retrieval; generic or reconstructed cues lack this priming value.
context: lab and applied cognitive-psychology studies, converging over 20 years

implications.text: Snapshot the centered passage, zoom level, and a one-line auto-recap at the moment a pause/interruption is detected, providing both a last-viewed highlight and a one-line recap.

observation: Leroy (2009) found people perform worse on a subsequent task when a prior task was left incomplete (especially if time-pressured or emotionally engaging) — 'attention residue' persists independent of how the switch itself was triggered.
claim: Riemann should distinguish 'interrupted mid-thing' (an open loop) from 'paused at a clean stop', since the former needs more resumption scaffolding than the latter.
mechanism: Unresolved cognitive activity from an unfinished task degrades performance on the next task, regardless of the interrupting event's own properties.
context: lab and field experiments, less HCI-specific replication

implications.text: Mark an explicit mid-L3 session end as an open loop (distinct from reaching a section end), and let the next check-in's recap say so explicitly rather than presenting it identically to a finished item.

observation: Amber Case's 8 calm-technology principles (periphery-by-default, center-on-demand, minimal attention required, graceful degradation, non-verbal signaling) formalize Weiser & Brown's 1995 'calm technology' essay into a concrete non-modal design vocabulary.
claim: The 'log silently' tier should be a genuinely calm, always-visible-but-never-modal peripheral artifact — a quiet log view with a minimal single-line representation, not a hidden inbox that grows into a guilt-inducing backlog.
mechanism: Information that lives in the periphery by default and shifts to center only when it matters avoids the always-vigilant cost of an ambient system, while still remaining genuinely visible rather than hidden.
population: general (foundational HCI design philosophy, not an outcome-measured study)

implications.text: Make the silent-log tier a persistent, low-salience peripheral log view with a single L0-length gist line per item, and cap or compress it so it never grows into a hidden guilt-inducing backlog.

observation: Retrospective analyses of Clippy attribute its failure to misjudging when help was wanted and being hard to dismiss/teach, not to the idea of proactivity itself; modern proactive systems (inline code completion, 2025 CHI proactive-agent studies) succeed when the proactive act is cheap to ignore, contextually well-grounded, and confidence-gated.
claim: Riemann's 'worth interrupting' tier should be confidence-gated (not just importance-gated) and always easy to dismiss/override, matching what distinguishes successful proactive systems from Clippy's failure mode.
mechanism: A proactive act that is low-cost to ignore and only fires under high confidence avoids the specific failure pattern (interrupting for low-confidence, low-value guesses) that made Clippy a byword for bad proactivity.
population: general software users (historical qualitative analysis plus recent CHI studies)
context: mixed historical/qualitative and recent controlled HCI studies

implications.text: Only fire a real-time 'worth interrupting' nudge when both estimated importance AND confidence that this is a good moment are high, and always allow an easy 'not now' override.

observation: A cross-domain study found users consistently report more comfort/trust in AI systems that behave as supportive tools (surface information, suggest) than in ones that act autonomously, even at similar task performance.
claim: Riemann's principle of never taking real-world actions is itself a trust lever, not just a safety constraint — it gives any 'worth interrupting' nudge a larger tolerable interruption budget than an action-taking assistant would have.
mechanism: The downside of a bad interruption from a purely-surfacing assistant is capped at 'wasted a few seconds,' never 'did something wrong,' which changes how much interruption users will tolerate.
population: general adults across multiple domains (single cross-domain study)
context: recent study, not yet a mature meta-analytic base

implications.text: Frame and justify the 'worth interrupting' voice/visual nudge tier on the basis that Riemann never takes real-world actions, which affords more tolerable interruption budget than an autonomous-action assistant.

observation: ADHD-linked time blindness makes people rely on external cues to substitute for a weak internal sense of time (removing all interruption/reminder mechanisms is not a safe default), while badly-timed interruption of hyperfocus is separately distressing; the literature converges on user control over interruptibility (explicit focus modes, quiet hours) rather than one population-wide policy.
claim: Riemann needs an explicit, first-class interruptibility control (a focus mode) that overrides inferred breakpoints, rather than relying purely on inferred signals.
mechanism: Inferred confidence-gating alone is not enough because confidence is estimated, not certain, and ADHD users specifically need controllable, not just adaptive, interruption.
population: adults with ADHD-linked time blindness (practitioner/clinical-adjacent sources, not RCT-grade HCI research)

implications.text: Give the user an explicit one-tap/one-utterance focus-mode control that suppresses real-time nudges and downgrades them into the next batch, overriding inferred breakpoint signals.
